chapters.title: a promise for the next life
chapters.html:
“May you be destined for a powerful fate, and may we reunite in the promised new world…”

Mydei doesn’t dare shatter Aglaea’s attempt at gentleness with him, even when he knows both of their fates. To die in a bath of warm and radiant gold, and to die with a wound in his back…neither of those promise a peaceful future. For Aglaea perhaps—one could hope, and pray, that it could be the fate of one who dies peacefully from old age.

But for Mydeimos?

There’s no such peace, not when he’s promised a death with his back turned.

It’s as he’s thinking this that Aglaea smiles, a mysterious yet knowing quality to it as she regards him. Instead of bidding him farewell as he’d expected, she adds softly,

“...where, I hope, you will realize that this magnetic allure you praise me for, has always been a quality we’ve shared with each other.”

He blinks. He thinks a confused smile must be playing on his lips when he breathes out a laugh, not knowing how to digest her words. “Is that so? That’s high praise coming from you, though I wonder if it’s deserved on my part.”

“You’ve captured the attention of the one you call Deliverer, which is no easy feat.”

“...”

Aglaea’s smile settles into something placid—a neutral expression that Phainon himself wears often whenever he wishes to pretend that he’s feeling fine, or when he’s hiding something. Mydei’s own smile has dropped, bemused as he is with her frankness. It’s one thing for him to express things bluntly, but for such candidness coming from one so experienced with the machinations behind Amphoreus’ prophecy and with Okhema’s politics?

To anyone else listening, they might think of it as a harmless comment. A simple observation that anyone else in Okhema could agree with: Phainon, for all his natural friendliness, has an interestingly close relationship with Mydei, the Kremnoan Prince.

But this is Aglaea. Goldweaver, and demigod of Romance.

Mydeimos is no fool, nor would he pretend to be one in front of someone he respects greatly. So he breathes out a sigh, and crosses his arms. “Do you speak of such things to Phainon as well?” he asks. Not accusing her, no—just curious.

She shakes her head.

“I believe it is not my place to guide him in acknowledging his own heart,” she says. “You, on the other hand…”

He laughs, the sound more breath than voice. He’d known that her golden threads could reach great distances and acquire a great many whispers, but to think they’d know something as mundane as his own heart? He smiles wryly. “You could tell that I knew how he felt, huh?”

“Indeed.” She tilts her head, and looks up at him. “Pardon me for my curiosity regarding your choice to keep silent.”

“What, you couldn’t glean answers from your threads?”

She smiles at him. “They can hear whispers but they don’t read minds, Mydeimos.”

“Hah. That’s good to know,” he huffs, more amused now that he knows she’d just been curious. It was interesting, to say the least, that their leader could have so much in her grasp yet still confess to feeling intrigue for something so plain and mortal. And who was he to not grant her simple request, especially when he’d likely never see her again? Thus, he confesses, “Call it selfishness, but I doubt it’d benefit Phainon to know that someone he loves is meant to die. To acknowledge it of a comrade-in-arms is one thing, but it might break him if he saw me as anything else.”

Aglaea hums. Then, seeming apropos of nothing, she asks him, “Did you know what he was like, before you first met?”

Mydei tilts his own head in question. He thinks of the Phainon he knows now—seemingly reckless, far too friendly, yet still hiding so many things within his heart. He smiles and laughs with his whole body, looks like a kicked puppy when he’s sad, and expresses a great many things with his eyes that one wouldn’t dare to think he’d have any secrets. Mydei had been told that Phainon was a man filled with vengeance in the early days, but it's not something Mydei has witnessed with his own eyes to be able to picture it in his own head.

He knows, but knowing is not equivalent to understanding. So he tells Aglaea, “I have a feeling you’re going to tell me.”

“He was… filled with hatred, and covered in blood,” she says, closing her eyes in seeming recollection. “It took many months for him to learn how to accept, and move forward, from his losses—and how to pretend, as you know.”

“Mm. He’s rather skilled at that,” Mydei agrees. He doesn’t even have to think too hard to remember any of Phainon’s false smiles; they happened too often for Mydei to forget them. “I can’t quite tell if this means he’s become stronger, or if he’s just become better at bottling everything up.”

Aglaea opens her eyes with a smile. “A bit of both, I presume.”

“Then it would seem my decision is the correct one.” He shares a smile with her, even if it feels wry on his lips. “May you be the only witness to this love, Aglaea. He doesn’t need to know—not until the next life, anyway.”

She breathes out a small sigh, before looking away. Softly, she murmurs,

“Let us hope that your love carries him over quietly into the next life, and that his love will find you in a more peaceful world.”

He chuckles. “I pray the same for you. Let us meet each other again in another life, where you will no longer have to carry such a heavy weight on your shoulders.”

She smiles.

“Farewell, Mydei.”

In the next life—

Mydei blinks his eyes open, and finds his gaze meeting with a mirror housing the image of him—young, cheeks round with baby fat, with eyes brighter and wider than he’s ever remembered seeing them in his past life.

Behind him sits his mother, Gorgo, who is quietly humming a song as she brushes his hair into a proper braid. She looks young still, with little to no signs of wrinkles on her beautiful face, and…

Mydei blinks again, and finds himself letting go of the breath that he’d been subconsciously holding in his chest.

“Feeling nervous, Mydeimos?” his mother asks, voice soothing as ever as she tucks a stray lock of hair behind his ear. He remembers, vaguely, having dreams of her in a past life where he couldn’t meet her. Yet now there was no need for dreams—not when she’s real, alive and warm as she wraps him up in a loose embrace. With a kiss to his head, she tells him, “We don’t have to go through with the meeting if you don’t want to, my son. It’s only a small favor for a friend, and nothing we can’t decline.”

“...No, mother, it’s fine,” he tells her, raising his small, child-sized hands to pat her arms in assurance. “I was just… thinking.”

She smiles at him, a glint of amusement in her sharp eyes as she gives him another squeeze before letting him go. “Ah, my clever son. What were you thinking about?”

He wonders, for a moment, if he should confess that he’d overheard the true nature of the meeting. That he knows his mother’s friend wanted to arrange a marriage in the future between him and her charge, and that it was only upon his parents’ insistence that the meeting be changed into something more innocent. A “playdate”, as they’d called it.

“Mydeimos is far too young to think of such things,” mother had said, voice soft after ending the call she’d been on.

Mydei’s father—Eurypon—had been a better father in this life than in his previous one. He’d quickly agreed with mother, saying, “Of course, my heart. In fact, we don’t have to set up a meeting at all, if either you or Mydeimos are uncomfortable. Why change it into a playdate at all?”

“...I owe this friend a great deal,” mother confessed. “A short meeting between our children need not be a promise of marriage. Mydeimos… he’s precocious, and it worries me that he has no friends his age. Let him decide for himself if he wants to keep this child as his friend.”

He decides to smile, and pretend he knows nothing. He’s only a child in this life—it’s not his business to carry the burdens his parents clearly wish to rid him of.

“I was thinking if I’d get along with the person I’m going to meet,” he says. “Do you know what they’re like?”

“I’ve heard that he’s rather bright for his age,” mother tells him, taking his braided hair and settling it over his shoulder. “Just like you. He loves to read poetry, and it seems like he’s excited to see our library. You could give him a tour yourself, if you’d like, since you know the place by heart.”

Mydei hums, thinking of the promise he’d made in a past life.

“If there’s a chance in the next life, you should come visit my library.”

It would be nice, if the child he’s meant to meet is that man he knew in a previous life. Though the memories are a blur given the length of life he’d lived before, he can still vaguely remember: pale hair and bright blue eyes, and that boyish smile hiding none of his mischief, yet all of his secrets.

Amphoreus’ Deliverer, and Mydeimos’ most trusted companion in his past life.

Phainon.

“It’s going to be a while before they arrive, right Mother?” he asks, looking up at her from over his shoulder. “May I wait in the library until then?”

She smiles at him. There is no sign of her old self—war-weary, roughened by life and cruel fate—as there is just her: Gorgo, Mydeimos’ mother, with a loving and indulgent husband, Eurypon.

“Of course, my son. I will call you once the guests have arrived.”

He grins, jumps up to a stand, before leaning in to press a kiss to her cheek. She giggles freely, no war nor treachery waiting at her back to stop her from receiving this happiness in full, and Mydeimos adores her so, so much.

With all that love in his heart, he steals another kiss from her cheek and says, “Thank you, Mother.”

“My darling son, no need to thank me. Now shoo, off you go,” she says, waving him off with a smile. “Have fun at the library, but not too much fun that you forget the time.”

“I will!”

Her smile lingers in his mind even as he leaves, and he finds he quite likes it. Instead of holding onto wisps of dreams and stories from Krateros, in this life, he can see his mother’s smile himself. He can hear her voice, feel her warmth, and know that she would never have forced him to be King even in his past life.

Because, both then and now, she only wants him to be happy, to live as he pleases. He knows this with certainty, even without a letter signed by her hands to prove it.

When he reaches the Grand Library, he gives the Head Librarian a nod in greeting before immediately making his way to the section housing their poetry. A poet, he is not, but that doesn’t mean he can’t appreciate it as an art. Certainly, he might not value (nor quote) it as much as Phainon did, but…

He chooses a book that feels light and sweet, speaking of love and gentle yearning, and makes his way over to the corner table that he always chooses whenever he reads.

Eventually, as he goes through the pages, he realizes that: where he could easily finish a book filled with myths and history, it takes him far longer to finish the book in his hands. Poetry is nothing so blunt and concise that he could easily grasp its finer meaning—he has to read once, before going over the words again, then again as he tries to comprehend the subtleties between lines.

…surely, he’s not poor in intellect? He’s always been praised highly by his teachers for being so quick to learn even at his young age.

Was it because of the overly romantic nature of this poetry book in particular? Making use of symbolism that occasionally makes no sense (describing your lover like they’re the sun while staring at them in the same breath holds no logic—would that not hurt the eyes?) was surely not something he could be faulted for not understanding.

“...you look like you’re having a difficult time while reading that. Want me to help translate?”

Perhaps because he’d been ingrained with the memories of his past life, Mydei does not immediately jerk despite the surprise he feels at the sudden presence behind him. Instead, he calmly closes the book he’d been reading, before turning his head to see who would dare to sneak up on him. The voice isn’t familiar, sounding far too young than what he’s used to, but the cadence. The teasing in them, surely…

His throat clogs up, eyes growing wide as he processes the vision of the boy in front of him.

“Phainon..?”

That same pale hair, those vivid blue eyes, that boyish smile—there’s no mistaking the young face in front of him, especially when the boy’s smile deepens at the name Mydei has blurted out.

“So you remember me, Mydeimos,” Phainon says, cool hands reaching out to cup his cheeks. It’s a brazen act coming from a child he doesn’t know in this life, and it’s brazen even with his memories, because he doesn’t recall Phainon ever being this free with his affectionate touches even before.

Still, he doesn’t bother to reject the touch. Instead, he raises both hands to keep Phainon’s palms against his cheeks, unabashed given Phainon’s own shamelessness in touching him. He asks, “How did you find me?”

“You said I should visit your library in the next life,” Phainon tells him, smile soft and sweet on his lips as he turns his hands against Mydei’s cheeks to take Mydei’s hands instead. With fingers twined against each other, he adds, “That’s why I’m here. It’s easy enough to find your name in this life, along with your parents’. Plus, well, I had some help…”

Mydei’s brows furrow. Though part of him is confused at the sudden deluge of sweet touches from Phainon, another part of him finds it reasonable. Phainon must have felt lonely after recalling the memories of his past life and his subsequent solitude after the fulfillment of the prophecy; it only makes sense that he’d seek out solace in someone who remembers him.

And, given what they’d left unresolved in their past life…

He squeezes Phainon’s hands, and asks, “What kind of help, exactly?”

“You remember Aglaea?”

He nods. “Of course. You’ve met her in this life, then?”

Phainon laughs. “Something like that. She ended up becoming my guardian in this life, somehow. I still have my parents, but while I’m here, she looks after me.”

“I see… then she’s here, with you,” Mydei says, a relieved smile settling on his face. While his heart and head are racing with thoughts—Phainon’s here, he’s alive, he’s fine—he’s mostly relieved to know that Phainon could make it to his next life and find him, and at such a young age too.

He’d have thought they’d find each other at the same age they met back in their past life, but it seems fate decided to be kind this time.

“Hey, I’ve been thinking about it, but aren’t you a bit too calm after seeing me again?” Phainon teases. That exact same cadence to his tone, that familiar taunting melody—there’s no mistaking his identity, even without the proof of his name or appearance. “And why does it seem like you’re more relieved to know about Aglaea than me?”

Mydei cocks a brow at the whiny quality to Phainon’s voice. It seems that he could still be childish, even while retaining his past life’s memories. “I believed you’d find me, Del—” he stops and shakes his head, “no, Phainon. There were no such assurances when it came to Aglaea, however.”

Phainon, as expected, brightens up at his words. Still so easy to please and distract, both in their past life and this one. “Once again, your words can sometimes be music to my ears. Did you miss me, Mydei?”

Mydei opens his mouth, ready to retort with a taunt of his own. That’s how they’re like, after all: they taunt each other, compete for anything and everything, and always do their best to not let the other have the last word.

But that was in a life long gone.

Now, in this more peaceful world, Mydeimos doesn’t have to fear the consequences of showing his heart a bit more than he should. And so, he says,

“I did miss you. All this time, I had been wondering when you would find me…and I hoped that the friend I would meet today would be you.”

Phainon stares at him. For the first time in a long time, he sees those bright eyes wide with surprise, and finds himself pleased to have been able to elicit such a reaction from their nigh unshakeable Deliverer.

Well, former Deliverer, that is.

“...Mydei, since when did you learn to be so sweet?” Phainon asks, voice faint from his mouth.

Mydei rolls his eyes with a huff, and gives Phainon’s hands a squeeze. If Phainon’s hands were not as cool as they were, he’d have likely released his hands by now—but they’re a comfortable temperature, and Mydei doesn’t like the idea of leaving Phainon’s hands so cold when he runs warm. “That was not being sweet. I was merely being truthful with you.”

“Your truthfulness warms my heart that I almost don’t know what to do with myself.”

Mydei gives him a wary look. “‘Almost’?”

Phainon’s bright smile returns to his face with a strength that could rival the sun. Mydei has to squint just to keep looking at him. “Almost, yes. Do you know why I’m here?”

“For a…‘playdate’,” Mydei says, the word foreign in his mouth.

“Did they not tell you the original reason?” Phainon asks. He seems to be pouting now, making Mydei feel confused at the sudden sulkiness. “Ah, I should’ve told Aglaea to be firmer about it… but needs must, I suppose.”

“...Don’t tell me.”

Mydei tries to tug his hands out of Phainon’s hold, and finds that Phainon won’t let go. “Phainon,” he says, scowling, “release my hands at once.”

Phainon’s smile only widens. “Hm, no!”

“What— no? Did you leave your brain behind when you went into this new life?”

“How rude,” Phainon huffs. For a child, his grip is surprisingly strong; Mydei can’t help from wondering just what in Nikador’s name they’re feeding this boy. Is he still training for war?

“Rude? You’re calling me rude when you won’t let me go even after I’ve asked politely?”

“Well, who knows if you’ll run away from me after I let you go?”

Mydei’s brows furrow as his eyes widen at the accusation in Phainon’s voice. “Run away? There is no such term—”

“—in the Kremnoan language, I know,” Phainon cuts in, sighing. “I’ve checked, both in this life and the last one! But that doesn’t mean it’s not something you can’t do, you know.”

Mydei sighs a long-suffering sigh, before turning his head up to the sky. “Fine,” he grumbles, turning his head back down to glare at Phainon. “I swear on my mother’s name that I won’t run away.”

Phainon promptly releases him, smile still in place on that terribly irritating mug of his. Forget missing him; Mydei is now recalling the many ways Phainon can be frustrating when indulged a bit too far.

Unfortunately, Mydei has often been very indulgent with him.

“Oh! Mydeimos, Phainon, you’re both here.”

Fortunately for Phainon, Mydei’s increasingly irritated thoughts are put to a halt at the sound of his mother’s voice. She looks pleasantly surprised as she makes her way over to Mydei’s library table, and for good reason: Mydei remembers her promise that she’d find him when the guests had arrived, and yet, Phainon had found him first. Then she steps aside, and—

He blinks, and sees a familiar beauty with golden blonde locks and blue-green eyes looking back at him. Gone are her white garbs, replaced by a black dress that’s fitted to her figure and just as fashionable as anything she could’ve woven in their past life.

Then she smiles and just like that, he’s reminded of the prayers they had shared with each other before parting ways.

“Let us hope that your love carries him over quietly into the next life, and that his love will find you in a more peaceful world.”

He chuckles. “I pray the same for you. Let us meet each other again in another life, where you will no longer have to carry such a heavy weight on your shoulders.”

“Ag—”

Mydei cuts himself off with a cough, remembering that he isn’t supposed to be familiar with Aglaea just yet. Immediately, he corrects himself with, “Excuse me. It’s nice to meet you, miss..?”

Aglaea hides what seems to be a laugh behind her fan. “It’s Aglaea, dear one. And,” here, she trails off, her smile gradually softening into something unfamiliar, something he’d never seen before in their past life. “...It’s good to meet you too, Mydei.”

He nods, smiling back. There’s still much he wants to say, and much more he wishes to ask, but he has to refrain with his mother’s presence in mind. She has no memories of her past life, and Mydei knows better than to let her recall a past where she suffered far too much.

“I see you’ve already gotten to know each other?” his mother asks him, her hand gentle as she pets his head. To Phainon, she greets with a smile, “It’s good to meet you, Phainon.”

“Likewise, Lady Gorgo!” Phainon says politely, a far cry from the menace that had been grating at Mydei’s nerves just a few seconds ago. “You’re just as pretty as Mydei!”

Mydei chokes on nothing. “Phainon.”

“Oh my,” his mother titters, reaching out to pet Phainon on the head too. “You’re a charmer, hm? Thank you, little one. I have been told that my son takes after me.”

Phainon grins up at her, shameless boy that he is. Then he dares (!) to take Mydei’s hand, wearing that ingratiating smile of his as he declares to all and sundry,

“I’ll be marrying Mydei, so I should ask you for permission, right? May I request your blessing for our marriage, Lady Gorgo?”

Mydei can only stare at Phainon in red-cheeked horror because what. Just earlier, he’d been acting like the same man that Mydei had known in his past life, but now he’d so shamelessly act the innocent child to—to what, exactly? Marry him?

He pinches Phainon’s skin from where their hands are clasped together. Phainon doesn’t even flinch.

His mother, because she’s far more easygoing in this peaceful life with no noose hanging over her or Mydei’s neck, laughs. “Marriage? Don’t you think it’s a bit too early for that, Phainon?” she asks, her amusement lingering in her voice. Where she’d been firm on rejecting the initial proposal of an arranged marriage from Aglaea, it seems that same firmness could not hold up against Phainon—and who could blame her? In her eyes, Phainon is just a naive child who likely doesn’t know the full extent or meaning of marriage.

Unfortunately, Mydei knows better. He knows that those big, doe-like eyes hold mischief like no other, and he means what he says.

Mydei closes his eyes, and sighs.

Phainon decides to add to his suffering by saying, “No, I’m sure I’ll like Mydei forever, so I want to marry him.” Then, with those big, blue eyes widened even further, he asks, “Please?”

“...well now.” His mother hides a laugh behind her cough as she turns to Aglaea. “I had thought you were joking that Phainon had requested it, but it seems you were speaking the truth. Your charge is certainly the precocious one, just like my son.”

“A perfect match, if I do say so myself,” Aglaea says, her amused smile settling more easily on her face than it would have in their past life. “But, of course, we would require Mydeimos’ input before we make any decisions. Isn’t that right,” here, Aglaea smiles at him, “Mydei?”

He squints at her. Of course she’s in on this. She’d been aware of Mydei’s feelings in their past life, and she made no secret of how she knew about Phainon’s heart as well. Perhaps, even when there are no longer demigods, there are still traces of the god of Romance within her heart…

Or she’s just a busybody, and has nothing else to do with no Okhema to watch over.

Mydei shakes his head, and barely holds back an instinctive eye-roll when he sees the heartbroken expression on Phainon’s face through his peripheral vision. Fool.

“We’re still too young for marriage,” he says, ignoring the squeezing grip Phainon has on his hand. “But… I’ll accept a long engagement,” he adds eventually, closing his eyes against the terrifyingly bright grin on Phainon’s face. “If that’s alright with you, Mother.”

“My son,” mother says gently, gaze soft and unsure when Mydei opens his eyes to look at her. “You must know you don’t have to agree to anything you don’t want to. Phainon seems to be a sweet boy, but you shouldn’t force yourself.”

“...No, I’m not forcing myself,” he mumbles eventually, tucking his chin into his chest and looking away from the ever-widening grin on Phainon’s face. “I like him too. But—”

“Ah-hah, no buts!” Phainon interrupts, a gleeful and toothy grin on his face when Mydei whips his head around to glare at him. “You said you like me too, so it’s final.”

Then he raises their joined hands and presses a kiss to Mydei’s knuckles, and oh.

Oh, he really has been too indulgent with him. Phainon wouldn’t dare do this if he weren’t.

“Hey,” he says weakly, trying to take his hand back. He fails, of course, because Phainon can be more stubborn than both the Titan of Strife, and the demigod that followed after. His face feels like it’s burning up to the tips of his ears, and his tongue feels heavy with a feeling he can’t quite name. It’s certainly not helping when he hears the giggling between his mother and Aglaea. “What are you doing?”

“Expressing my affection!” Phainon says—bright, so bright, that Mydei has to struggle not to look away. Phainon may be stubborn, but that doesn’t mean Mydei has to quail against him. “We might not be husbands yet, but it’ll happen eventually! That’s why, I need to prepare you for our future by being as affectionate as possible, so you’ll be used to it by the time we get married.”

Mydei clenches his jaw at the fox-like smile on Phainon’s face. He knows. Phainon must know that Mydei had reciprocated his affection in their past life, and is doing everything he can to make up for what he’d missed by being the way that he is. Was it pettiness? Grief-turned-stubbornness because he couldn’t properly receive Mydei’s love in the first life?

Whatever the reason is for his current behavior…

Mydei puts on a smile of his own, before leaning in and pressing a kiss to Phainon’s cheek. Just a chaste thing, something he’d do with his own parents in this life—and Phainon too, it seems, in the future to come.

When he pulls back, it’s to the sight of Phainon touching his cheek. Eyes wide and mouth hanging open, utterly awestruck like he’d been bestowed a great gift.

Mydei’s grin widens. Of course, no matter how wily and cunning Phainon might be, he still can’t win against someone who chooses to take the straightforward path. And so, Mydei teases him,  "Then I’ll be looking forward to it, future husband.”

Phainon’s voice cracks before he can even properly reply, and Mydei already knows he’s won this round.

“...I’m going to make you so happy, Mydeimos," Phainon says eventually, face flushed and eyes bright with determination. "I promise.”

Mydei lets out a laugh. He doesn’t mind the baffled and amused looks Aglaea and his mother are sharing, doesn’t mind the Head Librarian peeking in on them, and answers,

“We’ll see about that, Phainon.”

Let’s see who makes who happier in this life, Deliverer.
